title: I Love Zugzwang
summary: Make the opponent’s extra pawns obstruct its own king and rook; quiet rook moves force a decisive change.

nodes.question: Can White win without racing to capture a pawn?
nodes.explanation: White has one rook against a rook and two advanced pawns. Capturing material is less urgent than restricting the black king.

branches.title: Zugzwang: king moves
commentary: White has one rook against a rook and two advanced pawns. Capturing material is less urgent than restricting the black king.
Re4 quietly prepares an e-file check if the g-pawn advances. White keeps the king cut off from the upper board.
g2 pushes the dangerous passer, but now the rook can check from e1 without losing it.
Re1+ checks along the first rank. The white king prevents Kb2 and the rook controls c1.
Ka2 is forced: a2 is the king’s only legal escape from the first-rank check.
Re2+ is an independently supplied connecting check, rather than an assumed jump between source snapshots. It forces the king back to the first rank.
Kb1 is forced because Kc3 covers b2/b3 and the other a-file squares are occupied by Black’s pieces.
Rxg2 removes the g-pawn and reaches the separately illustrated zugzwang diagram. Black has no waiting move.
Kc1 leaves the corner formation and walks onto the first rank.
Rg1# checks along the first rank. Kc3 covers b2/c2/d2, and the black king on c1 blocks its own rook from interposing.

branches.title: The king escapes before the pawn advances
commentary: White has one rook against a rook and two advanced pawns. Capturing material is less urgent than restricting the black king.
Re4 threatens the same checking maneuver if Black pushes g2.
Ka2 moves the king immediately, retaining the g3 pawn as a potential rook shield.
Re2+ forces the king back to the first rank; Kc3 covers the nearby second-rank flights.
Kb1 returns to the corner arrangement. The rook still on a1 prevents Ka1.
Rg2 stops the g-pawn before it advances, and recreates the mating net one rank higher.
a2 is the illustrated pawn move, closing a2 and blocking the black rook’s path.
Rg1# checks along the first rank. The pawn on a2 occupies the black king’s escape square, Kc3 covers b2/c2, and Kb1 blocks its own rook on a1 from interposing.

exercises.prompt: Why are Black’s extra pawns a liability?
exercises.answer: The a-pawn can block its own rook, while the g-pawn can shield the white rook. Once Black must move, that fragile arrangement gives way to mate.

startContext: The full six-piece opening diagram is visually reconstructed. The king-first branch follows the illustrated Re4 ...Ka2 Re2+ ...Kb1 Rg2 plan. Three pawn-first branches include explicitly identified independent connecting checks before the separately illustrated five-piece zugzwang diagram; source snapshots are not assumed to form a continuous move list.
